AgentDefinition.description:
The complete, validated contract for one agent role (§2.1).

All eight §2.1 field-groups are required — ``extra="forbid"`` plus the lack
of top-level defaults means a missing or misspelled field fails validation,
satisfying TITAN-AGT-001's "a missing field fails CI".
AgentDefinition.title: AgentDefinition

roster_id.description:
This agent's declarative contract id — ``GET /agent-definitions/{roster_id}``.

The agents table and the YAML roster use DIFFERENT role vocabularies
(`backend` here is `eng_backend` there; `pm` is `pm_product`), bridged by
:data:`definition.ROLE_TO_ROSTER`. That mapping is the only way to reach
an agent's tier, supervisor or KPIs, so it is published rather than left
for each client to re-derive and drift from.

None for a role with no roster entry — the map is not total in either
direction (`orchestrator` and `critic` are runtime-only roles with no
agents-table equivalent).
roster_id.title: Roster Id

ApiKeyOut.description:
A personal access token. The secret is returned exactly once, at
creation; this is the durable record and carries only the prefix.
ApiKeyOut.title: ApiKeyOut

ArtifactVersion.description: One revision in a stage's history — metadata only, no ``body``.
ArtifactVersion.title: ArtifactVersion

ArtifactVersions.description:
A stage's revision history, newest first.

Not a paginated `Page`: this is a bounded per-(project, stage) history, and a
timeline that renders "v1..vN" needs all of N to draw itself. It stays small
because a version is an agent RESUBMISSION — one per gate-failure retry, not
per edit.
ArtifactVersions.title: ArtifactVersions

AssembledFor.description: Who the packet is for — attribution only, never part of the cache key.
AssembledFor.title: AssembledFor

Authority.description:
What the agent decides alone vs. must escalate (§2.1.3).

``veto`` marks a hard blocking power: only the Security agent (§4.11 / §7.4)
holds it in the default roster, and the runtime enforces it (TITAN-AGT-011).
Authority.title: Authority

AuthorizeResponse.description:
The redirect the BFF follows, returned as JSON so the server-side BFF can
read `code`/`state` directly rather than intercepting a 302.
AuthorizeResponse.title: AuthorizeResponse

BudgetsOut.description:
§8.4 / TITAN-SEC-082 caps. Named per_project_usd but enforced as ONE cap
applied to whatever project a call carries — there is no per-project override
table, so this is a single global ceiling and the UI says so. The windowed
tiers (project/day, org/month) and the local-time cap are Phase-71 additions;
``per_org_month_usd`` is the deployment-global monthly ceiling (TITAN is
single-org).
BudgetsOut.title: BudgetsOut

ChatRequest.description:
The canonical chat request (§8.1). ``model_alias`` is optional: when
omitted the gateway routes by ``metadata.agent_id`` then ``routing.default``.
ChatRequest.title: ChatRequest

ChatResponse.description:
The canonical chat response (§8.1). ``provider``/``model_id`` reflect what
actually served the call so fallback substitutions are attributable, and
``degraded_model`` flags a result served by a fallback (Vol 9 §10) so later
review logic can tighten. ``requested_alias`` is what routing first chose.
ChatResponse.title: ChatResponse

CollectionRebuild.description:
What reconciliation did to one collection. ``quarantined`` chunks were
skipped (dead-lettered poison awaiting operator replay); ``failed`` chunks
hit an embed/upsert error during THIS rebuild and were skipped so the
recovery command still completes (TITAN-BRN-004).
CollectionRebuild.title: CollectionRebuild

CurationReport.description:
What one curation run planned and (unless dry-run) did. Counts only — the
ledger holds the record ids; this summary carries no memory content
(TITAN-OPS-016).
CurationReport.title: CurationReport

DebtLedger.description:
The project's debt ledger — the open total for the dashboard plus the
tickets (TITAN-WFL-021).
DebtLedger.title: DebtLedger

EmbeddingsRequest.description:
Embed one or more texts (§8.1). ``model_alias`` defaults to
``routing.embeddings_default`` — the provider/model swaps by config only.
EmbeddingsRequest.title: EmbeddingsRequest

Escalation.description:
One ``must_escalate`` decision class and where it escalates to (§2.1.3).

``to`` is one or more targets: agent_ids, or one of
:data:`SPECIAL_ESCALATION_TARGETS`. ``co_sign=True`` marks a decision that
requires *both* named parties to approve (e.g. Backend's "new dependencies →
Architect + Security"), which the runtime enforces per TITAN-AGT-011.
Escalation.title: Escalation

FailurePolicy.description:
Overrides to the default §2.2 recovery ladder (§2.1.8).

``mode`` captures the fail-open/closed posture the runtime enforces;
``escalates_to_human`` (CEO §4.1: no supervisor agent) and
``watchdog_restart`` (Orchestrator §4.2 / TITAN-AGT-009: non-LLM watchdog)
are the other mechanically-checkable deltas. ``skip_retries_on`` lists
decision classes that bypass the retry rungs and escalate immediately (DB
§4.8: destructive migrations). ``notes`` records the remaining prose delta
verbatim for prompt rendering and audit.
FailurePolicy.title: FailurePolicy

Partial update — only the fields the client SENDS are applied

LogLine.description:
One structured log line.

``ts_ns`` is a **string**, not a number: it is a Unix nanosecond timestamp
(> 2**53), so JSON's number type would round it and the id, the cursor and
the sort order would all drift. Clients divide it down for display.
LogLine.title: LogLine

McpServerSpec.title: McpServerSpec

MemberRolesUpdate.title: MemberRolesUpdate

Replace the whole matrix. Partial updates would make "unchecked" and
"unmentioned" indistinguishable, and unchecking every channel for a

ProfileOut.description:
The signed-in human. §6.13 also lists an avatar — there is no avatar
column, no blob store and no upload path anywhere in TITAN, so this DTO
does not pretend otherwise and the UI renders initials.
ProfileOut.title: ProfileOut

ProfileUpdate.description:
Only ``display_name`` is editable. Email is the local-auth login
identity and the unique key; changing it is an account-recovery flow with
a verification step, which does not exist — so it is read-only here rather
than silently re-pointing a login.

``extra="forbid"`` is load-bearing, not tidiness: without it a submitted
``email`` is silently DROPPED and the caller gets a 200 with their old
address, which reads exactly like a successful change that did not stick.
Rejecting the field says so.
ProfileUpdate.title: ProfileUpdate

(``TITAN_PLUGIN_SECRET_<NAME>``) and an operator sets it there. A UI field
that accepted one would have nowhere honest to put it.
SecretStatus.title: SecretStatus

One row of the TITAN-WFL-006 traceability table: a brief feature through

Token accounting (§8.4). ``cached_tokens`` is the prompt-cache read count

Usage.title: Usage

UsageSummary.description: What Monitoring reads: the tiles, the group-by chart, and the series.
UsageSummary.title: UsageSummary

UsageTotals.description:
Money is a STRING on the wire.

`cost_usd` is `Numeric(14,6)` and Pydantic renders a Decimal as a string
precisely so it does not go through a float on the way out — a JSON number
would round the sixth decimal, and these totals are asserted to the cent
against a seeded fixture.
UsageTotals.title: UsageTotals

UserRequestSubmission.description:
The H1 UserRequest plus the CEO turn's proposed clarifications. ``topic`` on
each proposed question is the machine-checkable subject the policy matches
against canonical defaults and ``inferable_topics`` (computed by the CEO from
the request + organization memory).
UserRequestSubmission.title: UserRequestSubmission

WorkflowDefinition.description:
The task state machine (TITAN-BCK-012), served as data.

Vol 4 §6.3 wants a Kanban whose columns are "the workflow states" and whose
drags are legal moves. Both are THIS table, which until now lived only inside
the API: a client either hardcoded a copy (guaranteed to drift from
`transitions.py`) or discovered the rules from 409s. Publishing it is the
honest fix — one source of truth, read by both.

`states` is the canonical column order. `transitions` is exhaustive, so a
(from_status, to_status) pair absent from it is a move the board must refuse
to offer. It carries NO per-project configuration and no WIP limits: the
machine is global, and neither Vol 6 nor the backend defines either concept.

Legality here is necessary, not sufficient — actions additionally carry
server-side preconditions (`ready` needs its dependencies done, `complete`
needs a reflection on record, done-entry needs no unflushed working memory
and no Security veto). Those stay server-side and surface as a 409 with a
human-readable detail; a client cannot pre-compute them.
WorkflowDefinition.title: WorkflowDefinition

WorkflowTransition.description: One legal edge of the task state machine, as published to clients.
WorkflowTransition.title: WorkflowTransition

Direct KB writes are forbidden — always 403 (TITAN-BRN-021). Present so the
invariant is explicit and testable, even for an owner (``*``).

get.description:
A KB document with its full version history (§10.2) — older versions stay
queryable even though only the current one is chunked into titan_kb.

put.description: Direct KB writes are forbidden — always 403 (TITAN-BRN-021).

post.description:
Submit a KB proposal (§10.3 step 1): a diff + rationale for a new doc or a
new version. Never mutates a KB table — it queues a ``pending`` proposal with
its type-based routing and a semantic near-duplicate conflict check. Requires
``kb:propose``. ``proposed_by`` is the authenticated principal, not spoofable
body input (provenance, TITAN-BRN-021).

Approve a pending proposal (§10.3 step 3): the new version becomes current,
is materialised into ``titan_kb`` through the §5.1 pipeline, and KG provenance
is written. Requires ``kb:approve`` (the Code-Reviewer approval authority);
protected types (coding_standard/decision_record) additionally require a
HUMAN approver — the §10.3 human sign-off — enforced in the service.

get.description:
Structured log history from Loki.

Backs the Logs Viewer's history fill, its filter bar and its full-history
search (client-side filtering only ever searches the buffer). ``backward``
(the default) walks newest-first into the past; ``forward`` resumes from a
cursor and is what a tail polls.

A filter on a JSON-body field (``project_id``, ``task_id``, ``agent_id``)
matches only lines whose emitter bound that field. Most do not — the
logging context binds a project on request- and turn-scoped work, and
everything outside that scope is invisible to the filter rather than
excluded by it. This is LogQL working as designed, and it looks exactly
like a bug, so it is said out loud here and in the viewer's own UI.

post.description:
Trigger one §9 decay/prune/promotion cycle (also the nightly cron). Admin
only. Dry-run-first by default: the plan is written to the ledger; pass
``dry_run=false`` to apply Demote/Archive (and Compact within the approval
limit, or with ``approve_destructive``). TITAN-BRN-018.

§11.1 pattern miner (TITAN-BRN-023): mine novel patterns from a project's
decisions into project-scope pattern records. Admin only; the run is
ledger-visible.

§11.3 project→org promotion on the multi-signal rule (TITAN-BRN-024). Admin
only — org memory is never filled on a single project's say-so, and agents
cannot write org scope directly.

Fully reconstruct every Qdrant collection from PostgreSQL, reconciling by
point-id == chunk-id set difference (TITAN-BRN-004). Admin-only; runs
synchronously — laptop-scale collections rebuild in seconds, and the caller
gets the reconciliation report as the response.

Write a batch of Memory Events in ONE transaction — a failure anywhere
rolls back the whole batch (§5.1). ``source_agent`` records WHICH agent role
authored the memory (application data); the ledger's actor is the
authenticated principal, never spoofable body input (TITAN-BRN-005).

Authorization is scope-aware (TITAN-BRN-024): a human/service principal
needs org-level ``memory:write`` as before; an AGENT principal may write
ONLY project-scoped events into a project where its role bundle grants
``memory:write`` (its bound project) — an org-scope event from agent
credentials is a flat 403, because org promotion belongs to the curation
workflow's multi-signal rule, never to a single agent.

get.description:
The counts behind the tier tree and the facet filters (§6.11).

Counted under the same filters the list uses, so the tree never describes a
different query from the one on screen.

post.description:
Typed graph traversal (start nodes, edge-type filter, depth ≤ 3) via a
recursive CTE (§7.1). Scope-isolated: org + the caller's own project only
(TITAN-BRN-003).

File a structured lesson (§11.2): a protected episodic record + a lesson KG
node with a DERIVED_FROM edge (TITAN-BRN-019/023). Project-scoped
``memory:write``.

get.description:
Retrieval-quality and ingestion-lag metrics (§14) — the same series the
Prometheus ``/metrics`` endpoint exports, summarised for dashboards and
operators: packet-cache hit rate (TITAN-BRN-012) and ingest-lag quantiles
(TITAN-BRN-007). Metadata only — counts and seconds, never content.

post.description:
Assemble a cited §6.2 Memory Packet through the §6.1 hybrid retrieval
pipeline (dense ∥ lexical → RRF → rerank → budget fill), served from the
300 s Redis cache for identical (scope, query) requests (TITAN-BRN-012).
Scope isolation is mandatory: org + the caller's named project only
(TITAN-BRN-003).

get.description:
Browse memory records, faceted (Vol 4 §6.11).

The lexical half of the Explorer, and the complement to `:search`: `q` is a
substring, so it finds the identifier you half-remember, where semantic
search finds the idea you can only describe.

On §6.11's tier tree: `scope` is the only real tier axis and it holds just
`org` or `project:<uuid>`. "Patterns" and "Lessons" are NOT tiers — they are
records discriminated by `metadata->>'record_subtype'`, exposed here as
`subtype`. "Short-term" is not queryable at all: it lives in Redis keyed by
task with a 24h TTL, not in this table.

The canonical record + its chunks + its complete ledger trail (§14). A read
bumps access metadata and appends a ``read`` ledger row (TITAN-BRN-005), so it
runs in a transaction.

post.description:
Semantic search over memory, score-ranked (Vol 4 §6.11).

`score` is Qdrant's cosine similarity, NOT the §6.1 pipeline's `final_score`
— that one blends freshness and importance into relevance and min-max
normalises across the returned set, so its top hit always scores ~1.0 and
§6.11's "No semantic matches ≥ 0.6" state could never be reached. A cosine
is absolute and comparable between queries, which is what a score column a
human reads has to be. See `titan.memory.explorer` for the full reasoning.

A POST because the query is a body, not an identifier; it reads and writes
nothing.

§12 task reflection: one utility-tier LLM call answers the five-question
rubric and persists it as an episodic record for the task (TITAN-BRN-025).

List a project's messages. ``task_id`` narrows to one task's thread — every
state change writes a transition message here (``orchestrator.service.
_write_transition_message``), so this doubles as the task's event history.

**The two sender filters are not interchangeable, and which one you want is
almost always ``from_agent``.** A message's sender is recorded in one of
three mutually exclusive ways:

- ``sender_agent_id`` — set ONLY by an actor-driven transition, which passes
  the acting agent's id straight through. Narrow but precisely attributed.
- ``from_agent`` — a ROLE string (the roster id, e.g. ``eng_backend``). This
  is how the agent bus records every message an agent actually emits during a
  turn: ``bus.send`` writes ``sender_agent_id=None`` explicitly, because
  "bus messages identify their sender by role". So agent-to-agent traffic is
  attributed by ROLE, not by agent id — and two agents sharing a role are
  indistinguishable here. That is the system's own attribution model, not a
  gap this filter can close.
- ``sender_user_id`` — a human. Neither agent filter ever matches one.

Two further caveats. The log is HOLEY: a transition whose ``message_kind`` is
None (the scheduler's backlog->ready) writes nothing. And it is LOSSY: many
actions collapse onto one kind (start/block/merge/fail/... all become
``progress_report``), so what happened is ``body.action``, never ``kind``.

get.description:
A project's runs, newest first — the only way to ask what an *agent* is
doing.

``GET /runs`` requires a ``task_id``, which answers "what happened to this
task"; nothing answered "what is this agent working on". That question needs
runs, not agents: ``agents.current_task_id`` has no writer anywhere and
``agents.status`` only ever holds ``idle`` or ``paused``, whereas a run
carries the agent's task, the model and provider actually in use, its token
counts, its start time and its error text.

Project-scoped on purpose. A run authorizes through its project (TITAN-SEC-032)
and agents are org-level, so an ``/runs?agent_id=`` filter alone would span
projects the caller may not read.

Backs Monitoring's spend tile, its cost-by-provider/agent chart and its
time series. Defaults to the last 24 hours grouped by provider.

A note on what is in here, because an empty chart is otherwise alarming: the
ledger only has rows for calls that were actually made, and on a default
stack the live executor and CEO intake are both off (`live_executor` and
`ceo_intake_enabled` default to False), so the only writer is memory-ingest
embeddings — with no project and no agent. A quiet ledger is the honest
answer, not a bug.

Grouping by `project` returns raw uuids: `llm_usage.project_id` has no FK
and grouping by `agent` returns the gateway's routing key (`agent.ceo`),
which is not an agents-table id either. Neither resolves to a name here.
